red.summary: Learn why a legal decision maker needs jurisdiction, not merely influence. Separate the kinds of power needed to hear a dispute from the merits of the dispute itself.
checklist: I can identify subject-matter, personal and territorial jurisdiction
I can explain why a correct decision can still be unauthorized
I can ask which institution may decide a given dispute

sections.title: Power Before Judgment
sections.body_md: Imagine two neighbors disagree about a boundary. A court may hear their arguments only if law gives it authority over that kind of dispute and the people involved. That power is jurisdiction. It is distinct from the merits: whether either neighbor is right. A judge who knows the correct answer but lacks jurisdiction generally cannot issue a binding judgment. Begin any legal problem by identifying the decision maker, the legal source of its power, and any geographic or subject limits.

sections.title: Different Questions About Authority
sections.body_md: Subject-matter jurisdiction asks whether an institution may hear this category of case. Personal jurisdiction concerns authority over a particular person. Territorial jurisdiction concerns the place or connection within which authority may be exercised. These categories interact but are not interchangeable. A family court might have power over divorce matters yet lack power to settle a patent dispute. A court authorized to hear contract claims may still lack authority over a distant defendant. Always keep the three questions separate.

sections.title: A Practical Jurisdiction Check
sections.body_md: Start with the institution's constituting law: a constitution, statute, treaty, or recognized procedural rule. Then identify the type of claim, the relevant parties, and the geographic connection. Finally ask whether another institution has exclusive authority or whether several forums are permitted. This order prevents an argument about who deserves to win from obscuring who may decide. Jurisdiction is a threshold question, not a guarantee of fairness or of a favorable result. A lawful forum can reach a mistaken conclusion.

yellow.focus: Distinguish sources and limits of adjudicative power.
yellow.summary: Build from the three jurisdiction questions to the legal sources that answer them. Learn why consent, connection, and institutional hierarchy sometimes matter more than the label a claimant puts on a case.
checklist: I can trace a jurisdictional claim to its source
I can distinguish jurisdiction from venue and choice of law
I can analyze consent and exclusive jurisdiction

sections.title: Where Power Comes From
sections.body_md: A judge does not receive jurisdiction because a claim seems important. Jurisdiction must rest on an authorizing rule, and that rule may allocate disputes among courts, tribunals, agencies, and arbitrators. Constitutional structures may restrict what legislation can confer. Statutes may grant a court authority while withholding it from another. Consent may matter in some disputes, especially arbitration, but consent generally cannot create subject-matter jurisdiction where the legal system withholds it. A useful analysis names the source before stating the conclusion.

sections.title: Jurisdiction Is Not Venue
sections.body_md: Jurisdiction asks whether an institution may act; venue asks which place within an authorized system is appropriate. Choice of law asks which legal rules govern a dispute. These questions can produce different answers. An authorized court in one country may apply another country's contract law. An action may be filed in a court with subject-matter power but in an improper district. Moving the action to a proper venue does not necessarily cure a separate absence of jurisdiction over a person.

sections.title: Connection, Consent, and Exclusivity
sections.body_md: Jurisdictional tests often weigh a defendant's links with a forum, the location of events, or a valid agreement to arbitrate or litigate. They differ across legal systems. Some statutes reserve particular disputes to a specialized court; others allow concurrent forums. A lawyer therefore asks whether the court has power, whether it is the proper venue, whether another forum is exclusive, and whether any challenge can be waived. Never assume a waiver rule is universal: the legal system and type of jurisdiction determine the answer.

orange.summary: Move from ordinary allocation of power to cases involving multiple legal orders. Learn how adjudicative, legislative and enforcement jurisdiction differ and why a state cannot always enforce abroad what it may prescribe at home.
checklist: I can separate prescriptive, adjudicative, and enforcement jurisdiction
I can spot overlapping international claims of authority
I can distinguish recognition of judgment from its original validity

sections.title: Three Powers Across Borders
sections.body_md: In a cross-border dispute, the word jurisdiction may describe three different powers. Prescriptive jurisdiction concerns which conduct a state may regulate. Adjudicative jurisdiction concerns which tribunal may determine rights. Enforcement jurisdiction concerns coercive acts such as seizure or arrest. A country may prescribe a rule affecting conduct abroad without having permission to send its police into another state. Territorial sovereignty places particularly strong limits on enforcement. Confusing these powers can make a plausible legal claim into an unlawful intervention.

sections.title: Parallel Claims to Decide
sections.body_md: A seller in one country and a buyer in another may each sue in a familiar court. Both courts might plausibly claim jurisdiction. A jurisdiction clause may settle some private disputes; a treaty may allocate others; domestic doctrines may permit a court to decline proceedings despite formal power. The order of analysis matters: identify each forum's claimed source of authority, possible exclusivity, relevant connections, and any rule restraining parallel litigation. Do not confuse practical inconvenience with a complete lack of legal power.

sections.title: Judgments Do Not Travel Automatically
sections.body_md: Winning abroad does not itself seize assets elsewhere. A second legal system may require recognition or enforcement of the judgment under a treaty or local law. It may ask whether the first court had adequate jurisdiction, whether the defendant received fair notice, and whether enforcement offends narrowly defined public-policy limits. Those conditions vary. This creates a practical distinction between a judgment's validity where issued and its legal effect where performance is sought. Good advice examines both before choosing a forum.

black.summary: At doctoral depth, treat jurisdiction as a claim requiring normative justification, not only a checklist. Compare sovereignty, consent, territorial connection, and access to justice when legal orders overlap.
checklist: I can critique a forum's claim to authority using competing theories
I can design a jurisdictional rule that balances predictability and fair access
I can identify procedural injustice produced by forum allocation

sections.title: A Rule Can Be Valid Yet Misplaced
sections.body_md: Jurisdiction allocates power, but the allocation itself needs justification. Territorial sovereignty values mutual restraint; defendant-protective tests value fair warning; consent protects autonomy, though unequal bargaining weakens its moral force. A strict territorial rule may leave online injuries without an effective forum. An expansive effects rule may expose individuals to unpredictable courts. A doctoral analysis states the rule, the value it serves, whose interests it neglects, and the competing rule that could solve the neglect at a cost.

sections.title: Plural Legal Orders
sections.body_md: International tribunals, national courts, religious institutions, Indigenous legal orders, and private arbitration may make claims touching the same conduct. Their authority is not identical, and recognition may be contested. Legal pluralism asks how these orders coexist without assuming one system always exhausts what counts as law. The difficult question is often not which decision is easiest to enforce, but which persons should participate in determining the forum. A formally neutral allocation may systematically exclude poorer or displaced litigants.

sections.title: Designing a Defensible Forum Rule
sections.body_md: Imagine a platform injuring users in many countries. A plaintiff-centered rule improves access but multiplies defendant exposure; a defendant-centered rule improves predictability but can make redress impossible. A proportional design might require a meaningful connection, transparent notice, modest procedural costs, and protection against duplicative judgments. It must also respect binding constitutional and treaty limits. The task is to defend a workable compromise and say what evidence would show that it harms, rather than helps, those seeking justice.
